records.response_pred: I know. It's okay. Michelangelo is the reason we're here. Donatello is the reason we're going to get home. We're all just doing our jobs.

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. Three hours is enough time to do this properly — let's not leave a mess behind.

I know nobody feels like it. I know which one I'd rather be.

Donatello — when you're done with the notebook, can you do a final check against the inventory? I want to make sure we're not leaving anything behind that we actually want, or taking anything that belongs to the wreckage that someone might need for an accident investigation.

Michelangelo, I know you're watching the sky and that's completely valid right now, but when you're ready — even just gathering up the bedding and folding it into a pile would help.

records.response_pred:

I know this sounds weird, but I want you all to pay attention to the passage of time. Don't worry about minutes or hours — just notice when it gets dark, and when it gets light. It's a small thing but it's something we can track.

Now go. And DaVinci, I mean it about the water and food. I'm not going to feel guilty about it this time.

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

Michelangelo — it's okay to have that dream. It's okay to have that dream a thousand times and it doesn't mean you're running away or that you wish it had gone differently. That's just how this works right now and no one's judging you for it.

records.response_truth:
I believe you.

The problem was that you made a unilateral decision that the rest of us didn't get a vote on. You decided you were the best judge of when an emergency was bad enough to warrant it, and you kept that power to yourself. Out here, that kind of thing can crack a group apart faster than hunger can.

You're not a bad person, Donatello. You're someone who trusts herself more than she trusts other people, and honestly, given how competent you are, I understand why. But trust has to go both ways, or it's just control.

I also think you knew that and that's why you held onto it. That's not a bad thing. It's just the way you're wired.

Now we have a choice. We can put it away and hope it never gets used, or we can take it out and decide ahead of time what the emergency is. I think I know what you'd pick.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? I'd change how long it took me to check in on people properly instead of just redirecting them toward tasks. I kept doing that — someone would be struggling and I'd hand them something to do with their hands, which isn't wrong exactly, but it was also a little bit of a way to avoid sitting in the hard thing with them. It worked, mostly. But I think Michelangelo especially needed more than that, earlier.

I'd also push harder on the information-sharing problem from day one. Not just the food — the piano lessons, the flight path, what DaVinci was almost going to tell me and never did. We were all holding things back in different ways and it cost us something, even if we can't point to exactly what.

And I'd have had the conversation with you — the real one, not the task-management version — a lot sooner. You're not easy to reach and I used that as an excuse to not try as hard as I should have.

What's your answer? You wrote the question. You've had more time to think about it than any of us.
records.response_pred:
That's a good question to have. There's no right answer to it, but it's one you should get to yourself eventually.

If I'm being honest — and I'm trying to be — I think the question is also "do I trust you and the others as much as I trust myself, or do I need to keep a part of that power to myself?" That's the thing about leadership — you're not supposed to be the smartest person in the room, you're supposed to be the one who makes the room smarter. And the way you do that is by building a team that believes they can make the decision you wouldn't have made.

It's a weird thing to feel like you need to learn in a survival situation, but here we are. I don't know if you'll feel that way when you're back on the mainland, but I'm guessing you will.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. They didn't serve any practical purpose at all.

But I think that was kind of the point. Everything else we did out here was for survival — the water, the shelter, the signal, the rationing. The flowers were the one thing that was just for us. Just because we're people and not just bodies that need to be kept alive.

I think I understand that better right now than I did five days ago. Standing here watching that boat come in and not being able to move — it's not because anything's wrong. It's just that my brain is finally catching up to everything that happened, and it turns out there was a lot of it.

The flowers were DaVinci saying we're still here and we're still ourselves. That mattered. Maybe it mattered more than some of the practical things.

Why are you asking about them now?
records.response_pred:
Practical? Probably none. Not in the way that mattered to the day-to-day.

But I think — I think they were for Michelangelo, even if he didn't know it at the time. Because Michelangelo needs to make things that aren't purely functional. He needs to see beauty out here even when it's not in the obvious places. And DaVinci knew that.

They were for Michelangelo because DaVinci believes in the idea that beauty can be a kind of sustenance too — not just the kind that's obvious, like the sea or the stars, but the kind that's hard to see unless you're looking for it. The kind that's made by people who aren't just trying to survive, but trying to live.

So no, they didn't fill anyone's belly or save anyone's life. But I think they did something more valuable, which is that they reminded us what Michelangelo is actually capable of.
